decisions.reason: BASE preserves the source’s explicit four-character setup; “one phrase” drops that detail.
The standalone “Advance and retreat” supplies the four-character phrase introduced in H001.
SOL adds that neither side could gain ground for long; the source only describes the battle’s intensity.
SOL combines the two motivations without losing the lifelong faith or firm convictions.
The line about others’ firm convictions is retained in H004.
The source calls it a holy war outright; “to those fighting it” adds an unsupported qualification.
SOL keeps the point that religion no longer mattered amid the bloodshed.
The italics preserve the source’s emphatic standalone “Demons.”
The source gives each person a different standard of good and evil; “each side” shifts that to the factions.
SOL keeps the sword-and-saber clash, sparks, and indistinguishable shouts in tighter prose.
“Protruding halfway” and “inches from his face” preserve the arrow’s position and the tank’s alarm.
SOL preserves the near-fatal timing in natural phrasing.
SOL keeps Hunters’ proximity to death and their many past brushes with it.
BASE preserves the explicit action of snapping the arrow in two.
SOL retains the rain of flashes and the charging weapons and fanatics without changing the attack.
“Thought they might die” naturally conveys the source’s veterans thinking of death under the impacts.
SOL keeps the effort poured into their shouts and the deep furrows from their retreating feet.
SOL preserves the overwhelming numerical advantage in idiomatic English.
SOL combines the elapsed time, accumulated exhaustion, and the fanatics’ threat without losing their causal context.
The exhaustion and worst-opponent details are retained in H019.
The source says their number reached ten thousand; “nearly” weakens that quantity.
SOL drops the fanatics’ venomous, relentless attitude conveyed by their eyes alight with venom.
“Hidden from the world” keeps the concealment, and SOL preserves that they became another kind of monster.
The context identifies the pierced person as a fanatic, and SOL clearly preserves the blade’s path through his chest and back.
The source says survival is uncertain even with an immediate potion; “might not save him” instead suggests likely failure.
“Freeze” naturally conveys the Hunter’s body seizing up at the fanatic’s madness.
The chill is retained in H028.
SOL preserves both the chill and the belated realization that it was too late.
SOL keeps the sharp sound passing his ear and the immediate loss of sight.
“Bit his lip” matches the source’s action; “clenched his lips” does not.
SOL makes clear that the two comrades had repeatedly saved one another.
SOL preserves the dagger’s fatal placement and its taking Hans’s voice and life.
SOL retains the Hunter laying down the body as his expression darkens.
“Holding off” makes the canyon’s use specifically defensive; the source says it suited fighting a larger force.
“Saw death as martyrdom” preserves the fanatics’ belief in natural English.
BASE preserves the precise beat that the lines were about to crumble; “beginning to crumble” changes the timing.
SOL drops the source’s emphasis that the heat was intense.
“Fierce whistle” conveys the source’s intense piercing sound accompanying the falling fire.
“Fireballs” is a natural rendering of the falling balls of fire.
SOL preserves the open-mouthed spectators and the name flashing through their minds.
SOL keeps Magic Johnson’s reputation, Great Cataclysm record, and display of power in more fluid prose.
The fragment continues the preceding description and retains the spell’s potential to turn the battle.
“With that” preserves the hunters’ hopeful response to the spell without adding a condition.
SOL retains the hunters’ shared certainty.
The source says Magic Johnson could lead them to victory; “surest path” drops that leadership role.
SOL preserves that their confidence lasted until water rose from the barren, sandy landscape.
“Piled upon” preserves the accumulating water spheres and their rise into a tidal wave.
SOL retains the opposing forces mingling and then colliding.
The source says the shockwave shook a space hundreds of meters in radius; SOL shifts that to shaking the air.
The source stammers over “God”; “O God” removes that stammer.
The source describes one person’s scream; SOL changes it to multiple screams.
“Blinded everyone” naturally conveys the steam blocking their view, while keeping Magic Johnson’s understanding.
The clipped thought preserves that the spell was blocked almost completely.
SOL preserves the partial damage to the fanatics and the unexpectedly low overall casualties.
“Emerging under heavy guard” preserves their appearance under escort in idiomatic prose.
The omitted brow detail is incidental; SOL retains the low turbans, A-rank status, and combat specialization.
“Built the force” naturally conveys creating the overwhelming military strength before him.
The source says nature changed over thirty years; “landscape” narrows that image.
SOL preserves that gathering and training the mages is not the question he wants answered.
“Went to the beginning and end of it all” preserves the scope of his question in natural English.
SOL keeps the question about the Doppelganger’s motive for preparing everything so thoroughly.
The referent remains clear, and the omitted repeated name and “wondering” do not change the source’s meaning.
The contraction change is stylistic; SOL preserves that it had no time to answer.
The source contrasts his wish to chase the Doppelganger with his inability to move; BASE preserves that contrast.
SOL preserves the fanatics’ rigorous training and understanding of the battle’s key objective.
The context identifies the Hunters as the comparison group, and SOL clarifies the tenfold numerical advantage.
SOL makes clear that the fanatics concentrate fire on the Hunters’ strongest forces and commanders.
SOL preserves the relentless, dangerous attacks despite Magic Johnson’s rank as a Grand Mage.
“Much the same position” preserves the Skeleton King’s parallel predicament.
The Bone Sword term is preserved without BASE’s redundant explanation that it is made of bone.
The antecedents remain clear, and SOL preserves the flashes cutting through the falling bodies toward the Skeleton King.
The following hunk supplies the ten-thousand-person scale; this line retains his disbelief at their madness.
The fragment completes H072 by emphasizing that he had never faced so many of them.
The referent remains clear, and SOL keeps the contrast between his power and the overwhelming wave.
SOL preserves humans’ fear of death, his fear of Erasure, and the source’s birth-and-fate comparison.
“These humans” naturally refers to the people before him without changing the question.
The shorter thought preserves the judgment that the fanatics are the real monsters.
The Skeleton King is the clear subject from context, and SOL preserves the escalating numbers and attacks.
SOL preserves the blade cutting through him and the absence of pain.
The present-tense phrasing keeps the sword visibly lodged in his chest as he sighs.
SOL preserves the turned wrist, bone shard, and pierced attacker’s throat.
BASE preserves the source’s pause after he clears space, before the next shape arrives.
The Skeleton King is the clear subject, and SOL preserves the incoming shape and hurried catch.
SOL retains that the human is alive and coughing blood.
“One he knew” preserves the recognition in concise prose.
The recognition is clear from context, and SOL preserves that blood does not prevent identifying him.
SOL preserves the Skeleton King raising an undead monster with dwindling magical power.
“All looks” suggests handsomeness; the source teases him about having a good physique and little else.
“Barely above a whisper” drops the source’s implication that his voice was fading out.
BASE preserves the unfinished “don’t worry…” before the Skeleton King changes course; SOL completes the phrase differently.
SOL keeps the spoken praise with the action in one paragraph and avoids intensifying “remarkably well” into “damn well.”
The quoted praise is retained in H091.
“In place of an answer” preserves that the aura arrives instead of a reply.
SOL says strands drift down, adding that the hair falls; BASE preserves the source’s image of windblown blond hair.
“That bastard” conveys the source’s contemptuous reference without changing the judgment.
SOL retains the messy hair and cheek wound in natural phrasing.
SOL preserves the Skeleton King’s quiet laugh at the fury in the man’s eyes.
The source insists that Minwoo fought well no matter how the Skeleton King looks at it; SOL’s “No” answers the previous line as a contradiction.
SOL preserves the threat that death will reveal which of them was the demon.
The source tells him to come in quickly; “Come at me” changes it into a challenge to attack.
